item.title: cuBLAS Enhances FP64 Performance Using Integer Tensor Cores
item.description:
cuBLAS Enhances FP64 Performance Using Integer Tensor Cores

NVIDIA cuBLAS now provides automatic acceleration for DGEMM (real 64-bit floating-point) and ZGEMM (complex 64-bit floating-point) operations without requiring application code changes. This capability leverages the Automatic Dynamic Precision (ADP) framework to map FP64 arithmetic onto integer Tensor Cores while maintaining native FP64 accuracy.

🧩 How it works

cuBLAS breaks double-precision numbers into integer pieces, performs multiplication on the GPU’s Tensor Cores, and reassembles the results. Both the Ozaki and 2M schemes align input matrix exponents and convert them to a shared-exponent, variable-length integer representation for accurate accumulation.

Algorithm Function Efficiency Detail
Ozaki-I DGEMM Grows with the square of the slice count
Ozaki-II DGEMM Uses Chinese Remainder Theorem; linear scaling in number of moduli
2M ZGEMM Cuts complex matrix multiplication from four real multiplications to two

⚙️ Key details

  • Heuristics: cuBLAS automatically selects between Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II for optimal performance.
  • Memory Management: cuBLAS utilizes memory-parsimonious tiling, discarding residue pairs immediately after their corresponding GEMM operation.
  • Fallback: The system reverts to native FP64 MMA instructions if the required mantissa bits exceed library defaults or user-defined limits.
  • New Format: Rubin GPUs utilize the TI16 format (12-bit integer) to accelerate Ozaki computations via the tcgen05.mma instruction.

🚀 Performance Metrics

  • DGEMM (Ozaki-II): Achieves 5.5x and 3.9x speedups on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and GB200 respectively. Throughput reaches up to 175, 147, and 37 TFLOPS on VR NVL72, GB200, and RTX PRO 6000.
  • ZGEMM (2M): Achieves a 5x speedup over native Complex FP64 on the NVIDIA GB200.
  • End-to-End (CCSD): Achieves 2x and 1.4x speedups on VR NVL72 and GB200 using DGEMM with Ozaki-II.
  • End-to-End (BerkeleyGW): Achieves 6.6x and 3.9x speedups using ZGEMM with the 2M algorithm.

#NVIDIA #cuBLAS #GPU #HPC #TensorCores

Source: Faster Scientific Simulations with New FP64 Algorithms in NVIDIA cuBLAS | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Jane Street Implements Mamba‑2 in NVIDIA cuTile Python DSL
item.description:
Jane Street Implements Mamba‑2 in NVIDIA cuTile Python DSL

Machine learning engineers at Jane Street have implemented the state‑of‑the‑art Mamba‑2 sequence model using NVIDIA’s cuTile Python‑based DSL and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels.

🔍 Overview

  • cuTile is a Python‑based domain‑specific language and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile‑level GPU programming.
  • By abstracting thread‑ and warp‑level scheduling behind high‑level, tile‑centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores.
  • Mamba‑2 is a sequence model that aims for the best of both worlds: the fixed‑size hidden state of an RNN and the efficient, chunk‑wise computation of attention‑style models.
  • Jane Street, a global trading firm that uses deep learning for quantitative research, implemented Mamba‑2 in cuTile and worked with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels.

🧩 How cuTile Works

  • Import the package as cuda.tile and expose it as ct throughout the kernel implementations.
  • High‑level tile primitives hide the low‑level details of thread and warp scheduling.
  • The compiler maps these primitives to Tensor‑Core‑friendly matrix operations without the user writing explicit CUDA kernels.

🧩 Mamba‑2 Architecture in cuTile

  • The core recurrence is: $$h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t$$
  • h_t is a fixed‑size hidden matrix of size \(S, H\); it carries state across tokens.
  • Inputs per token \(t\):
    • x_t (vector of size H) – similar to values in attention.
    • dt_t (scalar per head, always negative) – controls update magnitude.
    • B_t (vector of size S) – similar to keys.
    • c_t (vector of size S) – similar to queries and used to produce outputs.
  • The output equation can be written as: $$y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}} h_{t-1} + D x_t$$
  • When processing a chunk of \(T\) tokens, the recurrence can be expressed with Tensor‑Core‑friendly matrix products: $$h_{t+T} = h_t + B X^{\mathsf{T}}$$ where \(B\) stacks the \(b_{t+i}\) vectors and \(X\) stacks the \(x_{t+i}\) vectors.
  • Adding the skip connection yields the full chunk computation: $$Y = C h_t + ((C B^{\mathsf{T}}) \cdot M) X + D X$$ where M is a causal mask, analogous to the mask used in causal softmax attention.
  • Removing the decay term reduces Mamba‑2 to linear attention with renamed components.

⚙️ Key Implementation Details

  • The implementation groups x_t, b_t, c_t, and y_t into matrices, enabling the use of Tensor Cores for the bulk of the work.
  • Traditional softmax attention scales compute and memory linearly with sequence length during inference, while RNNs have a fixed memory footprint but suffer from slow, non‑parallelizable training.
  • Mamba‑2’s matrix‑based hidden state and chunked computation aim to combine a fixed memory cost with Tensor‑Core acceleration.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By expressing the recurrence as matrix multiplications, the workload becomes memory‑bound rather than compute‑bound, allowing the fast Tensor Core pathways to be used.
  • The approach avoids materializing an enormous hidden‑state tensor, which would otherwise limit performance.
  • This joint effort shows how a high‑level Python DSL can bridge sophisticated sequence models and low‑level GPU hardware features without hand‑written CUDA kernels.

#cuTile #Mamba2 #TensorCores

Source: Accelerating Mamba-2 with High-Performance Forward Pass Kernels in NVIDIA CUDA Tile | NVIDIA Technical Blog
